Chapter 1
1.1 Introduction
Warehouse automation has grown around machines that move goods along wide, well-
structured routes. The aisle itself has received far less attention, and it is the part of the
building where the geometric constraint is hardest. A storage aisle is sized for the goods it
holds and for a human picker, not for a vehicle, so a mobile robot working there operates in a
corridor barely wider than itself. Clearance is measured in centimetres rather than in metres.
That constraint rules out most drive configurations. A differential-drive or steered platform
cannot correct a lateral offset without executing a manoeuvre, and the manoeuvre consumes
longitudinal space the corridor does not have. Once such a platform is misaligned inside an
aisle, recovering alignment requires either reversing out or a sequence of short forward and
backward motions, both of which cost time and both of which risk contact with the racking.
Mecanum wheels remove that limitation. Each wheel carries a set of rollers mounted at forty-
five degrees to the wheel axis, so the contact force has a component along the roller axis as
well as along the wheel’s rolling direction. Driving the four wheels at different velocities
produces net motion in any direction in the plane, including pure lateral translation and
rotation about the vehicle centre, without any change in wheel orientation. A mecanum
platform can therefore correct a lateral offset by translating sideways, a manoeuvre that in the
ideal case requires no fore-aft travel at all.
Mecanum kinematics alone do not solve the aisle problem, because a conventional four-
wheel mecanum platform places its wheels at the four corners of a rectangle. The chassis
must then be wide enough to carry that rectangle, and the width of the machine is set by the
wheel layout rather than by the payload. An alternative layout places the wheels non-
collinearly, in a point-symmetric rather than a mirror-symmetric arrangement: one diagonal
pair sits farther from the body centre along the vehicle’s long axis than the other. This
arrangement preserves the three planar degrees of freedom that make mecanum drive useful
while relaxing the packaging constraint that sets vehicle width.
The kinematic basis for this asymmetric arrangement was established in earlier work carried
out in this laboratory, which derived the transformation between wheel velocities and body
velocity for non-collinear placement and demonstrated it on a small prototype [1]. That work
established the geometry and showed that the platform moves as the model predicts. It did not
extend to a full-scale machine, to closed-loop velocity regulation at each wheel, or to the
perception and navigation layers a working warehouse robot requires. The present work takes
that geometry to a full-scale platform and builds those layers on top of it.
1.2 Review of Literature
Omnidirectional platforms and wheel geometry.
Mecanum drive is mature as a mechanism
and the symmetric four-wheel configuration is standard. Its kinematics, its singularity-free
behaviour in the plane, and its sensitivity to wheel slip are all well documented. The
asymmetric, non-collinear placement used here is far less common, and the prior work
establishing its kinematics for narrow-aisle application is the laboratory study cited above [1].
The consequence of the asymmetry is that the yaw lever arm differs between the two
diagonal pairs, so each wheel carries its own coefficient in the inverse kinematics rather than
the single shared coefficient of the symmetric case.
Heading drift and the need for closed-loop estimation.
Wheel slip is a major source of
trajectory and pose-estimation error on mecanum platforms, because the rollers present a
small contact patch and slip laterally by design. Galati and co-workers drove a mecanum
platform ten metres in open loop on industrial concrete and recorded heading deviations
between 3.98 and 4.81 degrees across ten repetitions, with a final lateral error of 0.79 to 0.94
metres; closing the loop on the same platform and the same surface brought those to 0.40
degrees and 0.17 metres [2]. In a corridor with a few centimetres of clearance per side, an
open-loop error near a metre is not degraded performance but contact with the racking, and it
accumulates within a single aisle traverse. Closed-loop wheel velocity control with a
measured pose estimate is therefore a requirement rather than a refinement.
Control of mecanum platforms.
Fixed-gain proportional-integral-derivative control at the
wheel remains the standard approach and is adequate when the plant is identified and the
feedforward term is calibrated against measured data. Adaptive and fuzzy-tuned alternatives
have been proposed for mecanum-wheeled platforms [3, 4], and fault-tolerant schemes exist
that maintain controllability with one or two wheels disabled [5]. Both classes of work
assume a symmetric wheel layout. Whether their results transfer to a platform whose wheel
pairs sit at different radii from the centre of mass has not been reported.
Simultaneous localisation and mapping.
Two-dimensional lidar SLAM on low-cost
hardware is a well-developed field. Graph-based methods maintain a pose graph and optimise
it when a place is revisited, and the widely used open-source implementation adopted here
descends from that lineage [6, 10]. Particle-filter methods carry one map per particle and
scale poorly on embedded hardware, which is why dedicated accelerators have been proposed
for them [7, 12, 13]. Scan-matching methods without a pose-graph back end minimise drift
going forward but never correct it [8]. Submap-based approaches with global matching are
more capable at larger scale [9]. Comparisons on low-cost rotating scanners of the class used
in this work report that scan-matching approaches outperform particle-filter methods on that
sensor tier [11]. The underlying mathematics, the point-to-line matching metric [14], the
nonlinear least-squares pose-graph formulation [15], and the Bayesian occupancy update
[16], are standard and are applied unchanged here.
Navigation.
The navigation stack used in this work provides behaviour-tree task
orchestration over lifecycle-managed components, with collision checking that admits
holonomic platforms rather than assuming a differential-drive motion model [17]. Its layered
costmap architecture separates the inflation band, which is a cost field expressing path
preference, from footprint-based collision checking, which is a separate constraint [18]. That
distinction matters disproportionately in a narrow aisle, because an inflation radius chosen
generously for safety can make a corridor the machine physically fits appear impassable. For
local control, the dynamic-window approach searches a velocity window reachable within the
robot’s acceleration limits [19], with known weaknesses in dead ends and U-shaped obstacles
[20]; sampling-based predictive control evaluates many sampled trajectories against a cost
function and handles omnidirectional motion more naturally [21, 22].
Chapter 2
2.1 Introduction
The second strand of this work concerns the environment inside the warehouse rather than
motion through it. Stored goods and the people handling them are both sensitive to air
condition. Reviews of post-harvest practice for perishable produce identify storage
temperature and relative humidity as the principal levers on quality loss and shelf life,
alongside controlled-atmosphere techniques that adjust the surrounding gas composition [27].
Carbon dioxide concentration is a long-established surrogate for ventilation adequacy rather
than a direct measurement of it, since indoor concentration rises with occupant respiration
and falls with air exchange, and it is used as such in indoor air quality assessment [28].
Particulate load affects both product quality and worker health. In Indian conditions these
quantities frequently sit outside the range in which either people or goods do well.
Two considerations motivated this strand. First, environmental variables relevant to storage
conditions and worker exposure are measurable but are not necessarily incorporated into the
control of air-treatment systems. Second, timer-based operation of treatment equipment
provides no feedback from the condition of the air being treated. Such open-loop operation
cannot adapt treatment to changing environmental conditions or indicate whether treatment is
required. These considerations motivated the development of a closed-loop monitoring and
control system in which environmental measurements inform both actuation and operator
awareness.
The system reported here was designed, built and deployed for this purpose. It instruments an
air treatment unit with continuous multi-parameter sensing, drives the lamp and the airflow
from those measurements, and reports over several independent wireless channels operating
concurrently, so that failure of any one communications path does not interrupt telemetry.
The redundancy is in the reporting paths, not in the sensing node or its power, both of which
remain single points of failure. The same architecture is intended to transfer to cold storage,
to controlled-atmosphere rooms used for produce ripening, and to general warehouse
environmental monitoring, which is the direction in which this strand of the work is intended
to develop.
2.2 Review of Literature
Environmental sensing in storage and industrial settings.
Multi-parameter environmental
monitoring is well established. Low-cost non-dispersive infrared sensors give carbon dioxide
measurement stable enough for indoor assessment, and an evaluation of several current parts
over several months found good agreement between them despite differences in construction,
factory calibration and price [29]. Optical particle counters give particulate mass
concentration, and combined temperature and humidity parts are inexpensive and adequate.
Non-selective metal-oxide gas sensors are cheaper still but respond to a mixture of reducing
gases rather than to any one species, which is why the index they produce is treated in this
work as a relative signal rather than a concentration. The engineering difficulty is rarely the
individual sensor. It lies in integration, in calibration, in keeping a deployed system reporting
reliably without attention, and in ensuring that the quantity driving a control decision is the
quantity that actually matters.
Communication architecture.
Facility monitoring systems typically choose between local
wireless networking, long-range low-power radio, and cellular connectivity, and typically
arrange them as a failover chain. A failover design must detect failure before it can switch,
and detection is the first thing to fail in a dead network. Running independent channels
concurrently avoids that dependency at a bandwidth cost that a low-rate telemetry system can
absorb.
Local processing against cloud dependency.
Cloud-hosted monitoring is convenient and is
the common commercial pattern, but it makes continuity of monitoring dependent on external
connectivity. For a facility where the monitored condition matters most during a disruption,
that dependency is misplaced. A locally hosted data platform removes it.
Chapter 3
3.1 Introduction
The third strand concerns the people working in the aisle. Physical fatigue accumulated over
a shift degrades both safety and throughput, and in warehouse work it develops under
conditions that make it worse: sustained walking and lifting, limited rest, and ambient heat
that in Indian facilities regularly exceeds comfortable limits. Occupational heat stress in
Indian workplaces has been measured directly, with documented exceedances of established
thresholds and associated health and productivity consequences [23], and comparable
findings are reported across steel [24], construction [25] and multi-sector southern-Indian
settings [26].
Fatigue monitoring as currently practised does not transfer to this setting. The established
laboratory methods are contact-based [30], and the established field systems address seated
drivers rather than walking workers [31]. The objections to instrumenting the worker instead
of the space are practical rather than evidential, and are given here as the design reasoning
behind the approach rather than as findings: a sensor worn against the skin for an eight-hour
shift in the ambient conditions described above is uncomfortable, electrode contact and signal
quality degrade with perspiration, compliance depends on the worker choosing to wear it, and
a facility employing hundreds of people acquires a daily charging and maintenance burden.
None of these is fatal alone. Together they are why this strand asks whether the measurement
can be made without contact at all.
The hypothesis examined in this strand is that information sufficient for the same purpose can
be recovered without contact, by instrumenting the environment rather than the worker. At
the time of writing this strand consists of a formulated hypothesis and a completed literature
survey. No hardware has been built and no data has been collected. It is carried in this report
as a proposed direction, and the implementation is described in Chapter 7.
3.2 Review of Literature
Contact-based fatigue measurement.
Surface electromyography combined with inertial
measurement is the established laboratory approach and gives good discrimination under
controlled conditions: a recent multimodal system fusing both through a hybrid convolutional
and recurrent model reports 87.9 per cent accuracy on induced fatigue under leave-one-
subject-out validation across 35 participants [30]. The requirement for skin-contact electrodes
and per-subject placement is what prevents its use on an operating warehouse floor.
Driver drowsiness systems.
The most mature deployed fatigue systems monitor drivers.
Thermal facial imaging alone reaches 82 per cent accuracy against observer-rated drowsiness
in a driving simulator by tracking forehead and cheek temperature [31], and wearable systems
fuse physiological channels for the same purpose [32]. These assume a seated, stationary,
forward-facing and cooperative subject at a fixed distance from the sensor. A worker walking
an aisle under load satisfies none of those assumptions.
Contactless modalities.
Several sensing modalities can observe a person without contact,
and their reported accuracies are the starting point for what a fused estimate could achieve.
Camera-based pose estimation recovers joint angles and gait parameters from ordinary video,
with mean absolute errors against marker-based motion capture of 0.02 s on temporal
parameters and 4.0, 5.6 and 7.4 degrees on sagittal hip, knee and ankle angles [33]. Lidar
gives three-dimensional gait measurement robust to illumination, and a point-cloud gait
benchmark establishes that the signal carries enough information to identify individuals [34],
which is a capability this strand would have to constrain deliberately rather than a feature to
exploit. Millimetre-wave radar recovers respiration and heart rates without contact,
correlating with a reference sensor at 94 and 80 per cent respectively [35], although those
accuracies are established for near-stationary subjects and degrade with body motion, which
the surveyed literature treats as an open problem rather than a solved one [36]. Thermal
imaging responds to surface temperature and therefore to thermal strain, and has been used to
detect exercise-induced fatigue directly [37], subject to the absolute accuracy limits of low-
cost sensors.
The gap this strand proposes to address is the fusion of these modalities for whole-body
physical fatigue assessment in an uncontrolled industrial environment. No study meeting the
criteria used in this review was identified. That review covered the publication record
indexed through Crossref and the scite database, searched between June and September 2026
on combinations of fatigue, gait, thermal imaging, millimetre-wave radar and lidar with
industrial, occupational and warehouse qualifiers, and admitted peer-reviewed work only. It
is a bounded search rather than an exhaustive one, and the claim should be read as such.
Chapter 4
4.1 Motivation
A robot that can work inside a storage aisle addresses a part of the warehouse that current
automation largely avoids. The aisle is where inventory is counted, where goods are picked
and replaced, and where the environment is least controlled, and it is precisely the space in
which conventional mobile platforms are hardest to deploy. A machine that holds its lateral
position in a sub-metre corridor, carries a useful load, and knows where it is well enough to
navigate without a human operator would make several distinct warehouse tasks automatable
with one platform: inventory scanning, environmental survey, surface disinfection, and cargo
transfer between a rack and a pick point.
The geometric premise for such a machine already exists. Earlier work in this laboratory
derived the kinematics for an asymmetric, non-collinear mecanum layout intended for narrow
aisles and demonstrated the principle on a prototype [1]. What that work did not establish is
whether the geometry survives the transition to a full-scale machine. A prototype
demonstrates that the transformation between wheel and body velocity is correct. It does not
show that four geared motors driving a 45.54 kg machine will track commanded velocities
accurately, that the resulting pose estimate will be good enough to navigate on, or that a
perception stack can be built on top without the asymmetry causing trouble. Those questions
require a built machine, closed-loop control at every wheel, and measurement.
This motivates the primary strand of the work: to take the asymmetric geometry from a
demonstrated principle to a characterised, autonomous, full-scale platform, and to measure
what the asymmetry costs and what it delivers.
Two further considerations motivate the supporting strands. First, a warehouse robot that
moves through an environment is more useful if the environment itself is measured, and the
instrumentation skills involved transfer directly between the two problems: multi-sensor
integration, calibration, real-time acquisition, and closed-loop control with safety interlocks
are common to both. Second, the people sharing the aisle with such a machine work under
measurable physical strain, and a monitoring approach that does not require them to wear
anything would be deployable in a way that current methods are not.
4.2 Objectives
Objective 1: Development and experimental characterisation of a full-scale asymmetric
mecanum platform for narrow-aisle operation
To build a full-scale mobile robot on the asymmetric non-collinear wheel geometry, to
implement closed-loop velocity control at each wheel with calibrated feedforward, and to
characterise the resulting trajectory-tracking and motion-estimation accuracy against
independently measured physical references.
Objective 2: Localisation and autonomous navigation at corridor-width clearances
To establish a pose estimate sufficient for autonomous operation in a corridor whose
clearance is comparable to the platform’s own turning envelope, to determine what sensing
that estimate requires, and to demonstrate goal-directed autonomous navigation on the built
platform.
Objective 3: Quantification of the cost and benefit of the asymmetric wheel layout
To compare the asymmetric platform against a symmetric layout of matched mass, wheel and
controller parameters, and to establish whether the geometric benefit is obtained without
penalty in tracking accuracy, disturbance rejection or yaw authority.
Objective 4: An instrumented, closed-loop environmental monitoring system for
warehouse environments
To design, build and deploy a multi-parameter environmental monitoring and control system
that drives actuation from measured air condition rather than from elapsed time, reports over
independent communication channels, and is applicable to storage, cold-chain and controlled-
atmosphere environments.
Objective 5: A contactless framework for assessing worker fatigue
To establish whether physical fatigue in warehouse workers can be assessed from contactless
sensing alone, without any worn instrumentation, and to develop and validate a sensing
configuration suitable for deployment on an operating floor.

5.2 Migration of the drive controller
Moving motor control from the Arduino Mega to an ESP32 was the first substantial change
made, and the reason is quantitative.
Each drive motor produces 93,132 encoder counts per revolution at the wheel, after the
optical encoder is read in full quadrature and the gear reduction is applied. At the rated speed
the output shaft turns once per second, so one motor emits 93,132 counted edges per second
and four motors emit 372,528. An ATmega2560 runs at 16 MHz, which is 16 million
instruction cycles per second. Servicing that edge rate in interrupts leaves approximately 43
cycles per edge for interrupt entry, register save, quadrature decode, counter update and
return, before a single cycle is spent on the velocity loop, the serial protocol or the safety
logic. A minimal interrupt service routine on that architecture does not fit within that budget.
Encoder counting alone saturates the processor.
The ESP32 removes the problem rather than optimising around it. Its pulse counter peripheral
decodes quadrature in hardware and maintains the count without processor involvement,
across four independent units, one per motor. The processor is then free for the control loop,
which runs at 100 Hz, and for the serial link to the host computer. Two further properties of
the part were useful: substantially greater processing capability and memory than the part it
replaced, and an integrated 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi radio, which allowed the first phone-based control
surface to be hosted on the controller itself, before the host computer of Section 5.5 was
introduced.
5.3 Level translation on the encoder return path
The controller change created an interface problem that the previous arrangement did not
have. An ATmega2560 operates at 5 V logic and accepts a 5 V encoder output directly. The
ESP32 does not: its input pins are 3.3 V parts with an absolute maximum close to 3.6 V, and
they are not tolerant of 5 V signals. The encoders fitted to this platform produce an output
close to 4.7 V. Applying the measured encoder output directly to a 3.3 V input exceeds its
specified limit and risks permanent damage.
All eight encoder channels, being the two quadrature channels of each of the four motors,
therefore pass through an eight-channel bidirectional level translator. The deployed hardware
is a discrete-transistor board with separate low-voltage and high-voltage supply rails.
One asymmetry in this arrangement is deliberate. Only the feedback direction requires
translation. The motor drivers have a logic threshold of 1.5 V and accept the 3.3 V drive and
direction signals directly, so the command path runs without translation and the translator sits
only on the encoder returns. Fewer components in the command path is worth having,
because a fault in the command path moves the machine while a fault in the feedback path
only misreports it.

5.5 Control architecture and software integration
Velocity control runs on the ESP32 at 100 Hz. Each wheel has an independent proportional-
integral-derivative loop with a two-term feedforward model, the first term accounting for
static friction breakaway and the second for the speed-proportional demand. Feedforward
parameters were fitted from measured open-loop data rather than assumed.
A Raspberry Pi 5 running ROS 2 was introduced as the planning and perception computer,
with the ESP32 retained for real-time control. The division follows directly from the timing
argument of Section 5.2: work that must happen on a fixed schedule sits on the
microcontroller, and work that benefits from an operating system sits on the host. The
software developed comprises a serial bridge to the motor controller, a second bridge to the
arm controller, the asymmetric teleoperation node implementing the inverse kinematics
above, an odometry publisher, telemetry logging, a scan relay that republishes the lidar scan
with the self-occlusion mask of Section 5.6 applied, and an operator dashboard served from
the robot itself with click-to-goal command entry.
The dashboard reaches the robot without any external network. The host computer runs its
own Wi-Fi access point, so a phone joins the robot directly, and one page carries the drive
joystick, the yaw control, the live map and click-to-goal entry. Whichever source holds
control, the asymmetric inverse kinematics of Section 5.4 are evaluated once, in the
teleoperation node on the host.
An earlier arrangement hosted a joystick page on the motor controller’s own radio instead,
and that was the first control surface the machine had. It was removed when the host became
the single command source. That path applied one shared coefficient rather than the two the
geometry requires, so it never carried the asymmetry the platform is built around, and it was
also the only point at which two writers could contend for the same wheel setpoints.
The cargo arm and the three-tube staged ultraviolet lighting are retained on the original
Arduino Mega, which was reassigned to the payload rather than discarded. The lighting is
sequenced on that controller so that the staging survives loss of the serial link, with a latched
emergency stop.
5.6 Perception and mapping
The platform carries a YDLIDAR X4 Pro, a single-plane triangulation scanner. Three
properties of the installed sensor were measured rather than assumed, because each affects
what the mapping layer can achieve. The scanner returns approximately 430 points per
revolution at 11.35 Hz and does not respond to a commanded scan rate. The manufacturer
states 2 cm absolute accuracy below 1 m and 3.5 per cent of range between 1 and 6 m, with
nothing specified beyond 6 m despite a 10 m rated range. That figure is a factory acceptance
condition rather than a runtime error distribution, so rather than extrapolate from it the
stationary scatter of the installed unit was measured directly. The robot was parked with
nothing moving in the room and every ray logged for 60 s; scatter is reported per range bin as
the spread of a given bearing’s returned range across consecutive sweeps, which is a different
statistic from the manufacturer’s mean relative accuracy over a fixed reflectance target.
Below 1.5 m the unit is solid in both captures, at 12 to 14 mm. In the 1.5 to 2.0 m band the
first capture gives 22.3 mm and a second capture, taken from a differently obstructed parking
spot, gives 31.9 mm, which fails the 25 mm half-cell criterion the occupancy resolution
implies. Beyond 2.5 m both captures return 55 to 200 mm and do not agree with each other.
Neither a linear nor a quadratic degradation model reproduces that pattern, since both predict
a single smooth curve. The behaviour is scene-dependent and is not explained by range alone
in these captures, which is itself the result: a range cap derived in one position is a fact about
that position until it reproduces elsewhere.
The robot occludes its own scanner over part of the sweep, because the mast and payload sit
within the scan plane. The blind sector was measured at five independent headings and is a
wedge of approximately 90 degrees covering 107 of the 430 returned beams. Those beams
are masked in software before the scan reaches the mapping layer, because an unmasked self-
return is interpreted as a stationary obstacle travelling with the robot.
Mapping uses a graph-based two-dimensional SLAM implementation, with occupancy
maintained by the standard Bayesian log-odds update.
5.7 Autonomous navigation
Navigation uses a behaviour-tree task orchestrator over lifecycle-managed components, with
a global planner producing a route through the costmap and a local controller producing
velocity commands that follow it. The collision footprint was set from tape measurement of
the built machine rather than from nominal dimensions.
The local controller was changed during the work. A dynamic-window controller was
adopted first, on the reasoning that it is computationally lighter. It was replaced with a
sampling-based predictive controller after the deployed dynamic-window configuration was
found to stall on rotation-only goals. Its rotate-to-goal critic invalidates candidates carrying
translational motion in the final phase, and because that configuration sampled velocities on a
full cross-product grid, only a small fraction of candidates survived the test. This is a property
of the configuration rather than of the dynamic-window approach as such: the critic’s
behaviour depends on the goal tolerance, the velocity sample set and the simulation horizon,
none of which were varied before the controller was replaced. The replacement evaluates
sampled trajectories additively against a cost function, so that particular failure mode cannot
arise, and it samples the lateral axis directly rather than as a coarse discretisation, which suits
an omnidirectional platform.
Commands from the planner, from the operator dashboard and from the manual joystick
converge through a priority multiplexer into the same inverse kinematics, so that manual
override outranks the planner at the single point where the two meet.

Three design decisions were responses to observed failures rather than anticipatory choices.
Driving the long-range radio directly from the host computer’s general-purpose pins was
attempted and abandoned, because the command protocol requires deterministic timing that a
non-real-time operating system does not provide, and scheduler jitter produced dropped
packets that were indistinguishable from radio link failures; interposing a dedicated
microcontroller moved the timing-critical work to where timing is deterministic. The cellular
modem draws approximately 2 A in transmit bursts, and sharing a supply rail with the
microcontroller produced brownout resets, which two supplies with a single common ground
point eliminated. The three channels run concurrently rather than as a failover chain, for the
reason given in Section 2.2.
5.9 Analysis method
Every recorded drive is analysed offline by a purpose-built set of analysis tools rather than by
inspection. These recompute position and slip from the raw encoder record independently of
the live estimate, grade a saved map against stated acceptance criteria, measure scan-to-scan
stability of the lidar returns, and verify that the coordinate frame convention holds across the
software. Building these was necessary because several of the faults encountered during the
work produced entirely normal-looking telemetry, and could not have been found by
observing the robot.
Two conventions were adopted after early errors and are stated here because they shaped the
results. Configuration is verified by querying the running system rather than by reading a
configuration file, and a prediction is written down before a test rather than after it.

6.2 Kinematics and motion estimation
The implemented forward-kinematic transformation was checked against independently
generated reference twists across twenty thousand simulated cases. The round trip reproduces
them to a worst case of 2.22 × 10⁻¹⁶, which is of the order of machine epsilon for double
precision, so the implementation is numerically exact to the limit of the arithmetic it runs on.
What this establishes is that the transformation is coded correctly and contributes no
numerical error of its own. It says nothing about the physical wheel-ground model, which is
what the floor measurements below address.
The odometry integrator was checked the same way. Position was recomputed offline from
the raw encoder record for a complete drive and compared against the estimate the robot
published live. The two diverge by at most 0.0054 m at any point during the run and by
0.0000 m at its end. The online and offline implementations are therefore numerically
consistent, which rules out a discrepancy between them as the source of the observed drift. It
does not rule out an error shared by both, since they integrate the same measurements through
the same model; that class of error is addressed in the floor measurements and in Section 6.4.
Endpoint closure was then measured on the floor against a tape-measured reference mark
rather than against an instrumented ground truth, and the precision of that reference bounds
what the numbers mean. Marking and re-reading a floor position by tape and eye is good to a
few millimetres at best, so the 4.582 m route closing to 3.1 mm, nominally 0.07 per cent of
path, should be read as closure at or below the resolution of the reference rather than as a 3.1
mm measurement. The 38 s square closed to 2.58 cm, which is comfortably above that floor
and is a meaningful figure.
Endpoint closure
Figure 10. Wheel-odometry trajectories for three logged autonomous drives, plotted from the recorded pose. Each drive

per cent of path travelled respectively.
Three complete drives logged in the test area are shown in Figure 10. Path lengths range from
8.00 m to 10.61 m over durations of 162 to 233 s, and each returns to its starting mark within
1 per cent of the distance travelled. The longest of the three, which includes the most rotation,
closes at 0.91 per cent; the two shorter routes close at 0.23 and 0.29 per cent.
The sub-1-per-cent figure should not be generalised past the route lengths it was measured
on, and the project’s own longest drives are the reason. On an 18 m route the same estimator
closed 0.229 m, which is 1.27 per cent, and on a second long route 0.257 m over 18.14 m,
which is 1.42 per cent. The honest statement is therefore bounded: closure stays below 1 per
cent of path on every route up to about 10 m, reaching roughly 0.1 per cent on short straight
runs, and sits between 1.1 and 1.5 per cent on the longest routes driven. Error grows with the
amount of rotation a route contains as well as with its length, which is consistent with the
increased lateral roller motion expected during rotational manoeuvres. Separating the two
effects calls for routes that vary length and rotation independently, which is a direct use for
the larger test space.
The yaw-consistency residual of Section 5.4 was evaluated across four analysed drives, one
of them a deliberately irregular trajectory rather than a clean circuit. Its median while moving
is 0.035 rad/s, with a 95th percentile of 0.111 to 0.124 rad/s and a worst instantaneous value
of 0.354 rad/s. No sample in any of the four drives crossed the 0.5 rad/s episode threshold,
which is the default of the analysis tool rather than a value derived from the drivetrain, and
was fixed before the drives were analysed rather than chosen afterwards. It sits about four
times the 95th percentile observed, so it detects gross events and would not resolve a slow
systematic drift. Within the sensitivity of this measure, and at the roughly one-per-cent
common-mode weighting derived in Section 5.4, the asymmetric geometry is not producing
the sustained wheel-fight or scrubbing that might reasonably be expected from a non-
symmetric layout. The measure is blind to a slip mode in which all four wheels slip together,
which is taken up in Section 6.4.

Self-occlusion

The self-occlusion measurement is consistent across five independent headings and is now
handled in software. It is stated here because it is a general consequence of carrying a
payload above a single-plane scanner, and because the trade-off between sensor placement,
sector masking and accepted coverage loss does not appear to be characterised quantitatively
in the literature.
Rotation and mapping coverage
Figure 12. Map coverage accumulated under three drive patterns, measured as occupied-cell count multiplied by the 0.05 m
cell size. The quantity is an occupied-cell equivalent length, a proxy for how much occupancy the map has committed to
rather than a physical wall length: a single wall rendered several cells thick contributes several times its own length, so the
totals exceed the perimeter of the room. Rotation in place contributes almost nothing: a deliberate 714-degree rotation over
642 s produced 43 occupied cells, 2.1 m on this measure. A 111 s arc combining rotation with translation produced 1545
cells, 77.2 m, which is 88 per cent of what a full perimeter drive accumulates in 18 per cent of its duration.
This is the most operationally consequential perception result obtained. The commissioning
procedure in use had specified rotating in place at each corner to survey the space. That
procedure discards its own corner observations: under the deployed mapping configuration,
rotation in place contributed almost no new occupied cells, measured across three separate
runs. The effect is a property of that configuration rather than of lidar in general, since the
thresholds governing when a scan is integrated and when a pose-graph node is inserted are
both motion-dependent, and neither was varied here. It is nonetheless the configuration the
robot maps in, so the procedural consequence stands: coverage accumulates through
translation, and turns must be taken as rounded arcs while rolling rather than as stationary
pivots. Correcting the procedure requires no hardware modification, and it was the highest-
value procedural change identified during this work.

Commissioning maps

Maps are produced repeatedly and reliably, and within the regions that accumulate enough
observation to be classified, the wall geometry they recover is consistent across the three runs
and with the layout of the room. Four acceptance criteria were defined for a commissioning
map before the mapping work began: that the map is not folded, that doubled walls occupy
less than 1 per cent of occupied cells, that unclassified cells occupy less than 50 per cent of
the mapped area, and that the robot returns to its starting mark within 0.15 m. These are
engineering acceptance thresholds set by this project, not values taken from the literature.
The 0.15 m return figure is the one with a physical basis, being the order of clearance the
target aisle geometry allows; the other three were chosen as the condition a map would have
to reach before attempting localisation against it was worthwhile. They are stated here so the
results below are read against a bar fixed in advance.
The three maps of Figure 13 are the commissioning attempts of 15 September, and every
figure quoted here is computed from the occupancy grids they show. None of the three is
folded, and return to mark passes comfortably on each, the best measured at 6.4 mm.
Doubled walls measure 0.7, 0.8 and 2.9 per cent of occupied cells, so two of the three clear
the 1 per cent bar and the third misses it by close to a factor of three. The spread is itself
informative: the run with the best coverage is the one with the worst doubled-wall figure,
because it was driven with the loosest lidar quality gate. Tightening that gate did reduce
doubled walls, to 1.1 and 0.9 per cent, but it tore the free space into disconnected regions and
the map was graded folded, so the looser gate was retained on the grounds that a connected
map with thicker walls is more useful than a clean one that has come apart.
The fourth criterion, coverage, is the one the available test area governs directly. Unclassified
cells occupy 73.0, 78.3 and 84.6 per cent of the mapped area against a threshold of 50.
Coverage accumulates through translation past surfaces, and the circuit available here is a
few metres of it, much of the boundary furniture rather than continuous wall. The robot
classifies what it drives past, so the figure is a statement about the space rather than about the
mapping layer.
The denominator matters and is stated here because it qualifies the figure. The percentage is
computed over every cell in the published occupancy grid, which is the bounding extent the
mapper has allocated rather than the traversable floor area. Cells the robot could never reach
or see are counted in the denominator, so the figure is sensitive to how large a window the
mapper happens to allocate and overstates the fraction of reachable space left unobserved. It
is used here because it is the criterion that was written down before the mapping work began
and because the same definition applies to every run compared, which makes the run-to-run
comparison valid even where the absolute number is soft. A coverage criterion computed
over a fixed region of interest corresponding to the traversable area would be the better
measure and is owed.
Coverage is the criterion that fails on all three runs, and the dominant limiting mechanism is
consistent with the coverage dependence measured in Section 6.3 and with the restricted
geometry of the available test area. Coverage accumulates through translation past surfaces,
at a rate set by how much distance the robot can travel while observing new geometry. The
laboratory area available for this work permits a traversable circuit of only a few metres,
much of it bounded by furniture rather than by continuous wall. A drive confined to that
circuit cannot accumulate the observation the coverage criterion requires, however well the
platform performs, because the criterion is a statement about how much of the mapped area
has been seen and the robot cannot see what it cannot drive past.
What follows is concrete in kind if not yet in magnitude. Validating the mapping and
localisation layers requires a test space offering a continuous traversable loop with
unobstructed wall on at least one side and aisle widths representative of the target application.
An initial target of fifteen to twenty metres of path is proposed on the grounds that it is
several times the few metres currently available, not derived from a measured coverage-
accumulation rate; establishing that rate, and with it the path length a 50 per cent coverage
criterion actually demands, is itself one of the first measurements the new space would
support. Securing such a space is the principal practical prerequisite for the next stage of the
work, and it is the reason the localisation mode that depends on a saved map has not yet been
exercised.

Heading at
the end of a drive was measured from video against world-static floor features, using tile-
grout orientation as the reference, since the alignment criterion used throughout this work is
the chassis edge parallel to the tile line. Frames were extracted with ffmpeg, position taken
from a threshold centroid on floor brackets, and heading from a gradient-orientation
histogram on the grout lines. The instrument was validated before its output was believed, on
frames where the commanded rotation was known: it returned −27.07° against a commanded
−28.0°, and −18.50° against −19.4°, agreeing within one degree in both cases. That
agreement is the only uncertainty estimate available for the method, so its resolution is taken
as of order one degree, which is what makes the 3.85° and 4.49° results below interpretable:
they are several times the instrument’s demonstrated agreement, not comparable to it. Two
failure modes were found and corrected during that validation, the first of them measuring the
robot against a camera mounted on the robot’s own mast, which by construction reports no
rotation at all.
On two structurally different routes the robot finished 3.85° and 4.49° away from its
commanded heading, while wheel odometry, the published estimate and the SLAM pose all
agreed with one another to within a few hundredths of a degree. Three estimates agreeing
while all three disagree with the floor is the signature of an error they share, not one that
separates them.
What that narrows the error to should be stated carefully, because the obvious reading is
stronger than the evidence. The yaw-consistency residual rules out significant differential slip
between wheels, and the offline re-integration rules out an integration fault. The two leading
candidates that remain are an encoder or wheel-radius scale error, which is estimator error
and is recoverable by calibration, and a slip mode in which all four wheels slip together and
the platform’s motion stays rigid, which is physical and is not. The elimination is not
exhaustive: a geometric parameter error, a systematic mounting offset or a timing error
between the encoder and pose streams would produce a similar signature and have not been
separately excluded. No instrument currently fitted to the robot can distinguish any of them.
That is the specific reason an independent heading reference is the next measurement rather
than a general improvement, and it is taken up in Section 6.6.
6.5 Autonomous navigation
Autonomous point-to-point navigation has been demonstrated on the platform within a live
mapping session. The demonstration is preliminary and the number of trials is small, so it is
reported as what it is rather than as a validated capability. The first complete autonomous
round trip was performed in August: the robot drove out, reversed its heading and returned,
holding direction to within 5.5 and 3.7 degrees on the two legs and stopping 4.6 cm short of
the commanded stop point. In later trials goals were selected by tapping the map in the
dashboard and the platform reached them in 21 and 26 s respectively. Three goals were
commanded across three trials and all three were reached. Establishing a success rate, a
stopping-error distribution and behaviour against obstacles requires a larger trial count in a
space that permits varied routes, which places this alongside the mapping work behind the
same test-space constraint.
The operator interface was verified geometrically rather than by eye. The transformation
from a tapped screen pixel to a world coordinate was tested across the full round trip against
its analytic value at three different display pixel densities, and agrees to within one part in a
million, which over the extent of the test map is well under a millimetre. This is a check that
the transformation is coded correctly, not a statement about pointing accuracy, which is set by
the size of a fingertip against the map scale and was not measured.
Navigation currently operates within a live mapping session rather than against a previously
saved map, for the reason given in Section 6.4.
6.6 Operating without an inertial sensor
The platform carries no inertial measurement unit. That was a decision rather than an
omission, and it is worth setting out, because it is the first question the estimator results
invite.
Objective 2 asks for a pose estimate characterised against an independently measured
physical reference, with a stated drift figure over a stated distance and an explicit account of
which sensors are required to reach it. The third clause is the research content, and it is a
question about sensors rather than a requirement to own one. Fitting inertial measurement at
the start would have removed the ability to answer it. Fusion improves the estimate; without a
characterised unfused baseline at the operating scale there is no way to say by how much, or
which error it removed. The unfused platform is that baseline.
Which instrument binds the error at the 5 m operating scale is not something this year’s data
settles, and the report does not claim it does. Endpoint closure was not measured at 5 m: the
routes driven were either short and straight, closing to roughly 0.1 per cent, or long and
rotation-heavy, closing at 1.1 to 1.5 per cent, and applying either rate to an intermediate
distance is extrapolation rather than measurement. The scanner is characterised on its own
terms instead. Its stationary ray scatter is 22.3 mm in the 1.5 to 2.0 m band in one 60 s
capture and 31.9 mm in a second capture taken from a differently obstructed position, the
latter failing the 25 mm half-cell criterion the mapping configuration implies. Beyond 2.5 m
neither capture agrees with the other. What that establishes is that the scanner is unreliable at
the ranges a corridor-width map depends on, not that it is the larger of two quantified error
terms. Both estimators have limitations at the intended scale, and separating their
contributions needs the third measurement an inertial sensor would provide.
What an inertial sensor would add is specific, and the measurement of Section 6.4 gives it a
target. Heading errors of 3.85° and 4.49° were invisible to every instrument on the robot,
because all of them derive from the same wheel measurements. A rate gyroscope measures
angular rate independently of the wheels; integrating it gives a heading estimate that drifts
with bias but that does not share the wheel-derived error, and that is what would make this
class of error observable and separate an encoder scale error from a rigid all-wheel slip mode.
That is the falsifiable test, and it can only be run against a baseline that already exists.
What is not claimed is that the platform is better off without one. Fusion would reduce
heading error, an inertial sensor is the right next purchase, and nothing here argues otherwise.
The claim is about order of work. Objective 2 therefore closes as characterised rather than as
optimal, and inertial measurement with fused state estimation is the first item of Chapter 7,
now carrying a specific number to be tested against rather than a general expectation.

clean, the kinematic and odometry implementations are numerically consistent to machine
precision across the cases tested, the frame composition reproduces to four decimal places,
the planner plans, the local controller reaches goals, and the operator interface is
geometrically correct. Wheel odometry, which is the least expensive sensing on the platform,
is currently its most extensively characterised source of state estimation.
Figure 14 states the evidence against every layer, and what it shows is that the work still open
resolves to two constraints rather than to a list of separate shortfalls.
The first is the size of the available test area.
Coverage accumulates through translation
past surfaces, at a rate set by how far the robot can drive while observing new geometry, and
the laboratory available for this work permits a traversable circuit of only a few metres. That
single limit propagates: it holds the coverage criterion below its threshold, which withholds
an accepted commissioning map, which in turn leaves localisation against a saved map
unexercised and gives the named-location library no coordinates to store. Four entries in
Figure 14, and one cause. No further work on the platform moves any of them, and a test
space offering a continuous traversable loop lifts all four together.
The second is the deliberate absence of inertial measurement
, for the reason set out in
Section 6.6. Working without it is what made the unfused baseline measurable, and the cost is
one specific error class that stays unobservable to a wheel-only instrument set. Adding the
sensor is the first item of Chapter 7 and it now has a measured target to be tested against.
Three further components, the global planner, the local controller and the safety chain, work
correctly but run below their requested update rates because of the processing available on
the host computer. That is a property of the computer rather than of the software, and a faster
host raises all three.
Scan matching is the one entry that is switched off by choice rather than by constraint, on the
measurement reported in Section 6.4.
6.8 Environmental monitoring system
The monitoring system is deployed and operating across four zones in two radio-isolated
installations sharing one database. All three communication channels, both control paths and
the dashboards are in service, and the system recovers automatically after a power
interruption without intervention.
The control law was checked against the deployed system rather than asserted, although what
that check establishes should be stated precisely. A dashboard capture taken during operation
shows the gas index below the configured actuation threshold with the lamp correspondingly
off, and the carbon dioxide reading at the same instant above its alert threshold with the node
having raised an alert on all three channels. That is a single consistent operating state, and it
demonstrates that the deployed logic produces the configured actuator and alert states for the
inputs present at that instant. It is not a time-resolved measurement of the loop responding to
a change, which would require logging the measurement, the threshold crossing, the actuator
command and the resulting response on one time axis. That recording has not been made.
One limitation is recorded plainly. The non-selective gas index that drives the present control
law is a relative signal rather than a calibrated concentration, adequate for actuation and trend
observation but not for any quantitative claim. This is documented, and addressing it is part
of the work described in Chapter 7.
Chapter 7
7.1 Future Work
Securing a representative test space.
The coverage limitation of Section 6.4 is the binding
constraint on the mapping and localisation layers, and it is environmental rather than
technical. A continuous traversable loop with unobstructed wall on at least one side and aisle
widths representative of the application is required before the commissioning criteria can be
assessed meaningfully. An initial target of fifteen to twenty metres of path is proposed, on the
grounds that it is several times the few metres currently available rather than derived from a
measured coverage-accumulation rate. Arranging access to such a space is the first practical
task.
Inertial measurement and fused state estimation.
The photogrammetric result of Section
6.4 leaves two candidate explanations for several degrees of heading error that every fitted
instrument misses: an encoder or wheel-radius scale error, which calibration can remove, or a
rigid slip mode in which all four wheels slip together, which it cannot. Separating them needs
an angular-rate measurement that does not derive from the wheels. Adding an inertial sensor
near the geometric centre, where the rotationally induced terms in the accelerometer channel
are smallest, and fusing its integrated rate with the wheel estimate is the direct response, and
for the reason given in Section 6.6 it is the right next step rather than something that should
have come first. The 3.85° and 4.49° already measured give a specific quantity against which
the improvement can be tested.
Sensor comparison.
The case against the present lidar is now quantitative rather than
impressionistic. Repeating the same routes with a higher-grade scanner, using the same
analysis tools, would convert that inference into a controlled result and would establish what
sensing this class of platform actually requires. That question is currently answered in the
literature by convention rather than by measurement.
Completing the geometric comparison.
No asymmetry-specific penalty has been detected
in any experiment performed so far: the transformation is implemented correctly to the limit
of double precision, tracking is clean on every axis including lateral and rotational motion,
endpoint closure holds below 1 per cent on the three logged drives up to 10.61 m and to 1.1
to 1.5 per cent on the longest routes driven, and no yaw-consistency residual above the
episode threshold has been observed. A matched symmetric baseline has not been tested, so
the effect of the asymmetry itself remains unquantified. What has not been performed is a
controlled side-by-side comparison against a symmetric layout of matched mass, wheel and
controller parameters. Building that baseline, in simulation first and on hardware if the
wheelbase can be reconfigured without a new chassis, would convert a consistent absence of
penalty into a measured result and would close Objective 3.
Extending the platform to warehouse tasks.
The chassis is intended as a general-purpose
autonomous base, with task capability delivered by attachments. Inventory scanning,
environmental survey, surface disinfection and cargo transfer are the intended applications,
and each requires integration work on top of the autonomy layer rather than changes to it.
Developing the monitoring system toward storage applications.
The architecture is
intended to transfer beyond the unit it was built for. Cold-chain storage, controlled-
atmosphere rooms used for produce ripening, and general warehouse environmental survey
call for the same measurement set and the same resilience to intermittent connectivity,
although the system has so far been deployed in one application and transferability is a design
expectation rather than a demonstrated result. Traceable calibration of the measurement
channels and a buffered store-and-forward path, so that an outage costs latency rather than
data, are the next steps.
Implementing the contactless fatigue framework.
This strand currently consists of a
hypothesis and a completed literature survey. The implementation begins with a single-
subject capture arrangement at a fixed location, such as an aisle end or doorway, so that each
crossing yields one clean measurement rather than requiring continuous tracking of several
people at once. Laboratory validation of each modality against a direct physical measure of
fatigue precedes any deployment, and the fused estimate must be shown to outperform a
simple baseline derived from ambient conditions and hours worked before the approach can
be considered established.
7.2 Year-One Conclusions
The year produced a full-scale asymmetric mecanum platform with calibrated wheel-level
control, an implementation of the non-collinear kinematics verified against an independent
reference, wheel odometry characterised against physical floor marks, a measured account of
the scanner’s limitations, a preliminary demonstration of autonomous navigation, and a
deployed environmental monitoring system operating across four zones.
Four results are established rather than asserted. The velocity controller tracks to 0.040 to
0.047 rad/s root-mean-square unloaded and 0.066 to 0.074 under chassis weight, with no
channel saturating in any recorded run. The kinematic and odometry implementations are
numerically consistent to machine precision across twenty thousand generated cases and
against an offline re-integration of a complete drive. Wheel-odometry endpoint closure stays
below 1 per cent of path to about 10 m and sits between 1.1 and 1.5 per cent on the longest
routes driven. Scan matching was measured to increase pose error on three separate routes,
most tightly on a drive where the same wheels and the same scans gave 16.2 mm unmatched
and 206.7 mm matched, with corrections firing on a fixed odometry cadence rather than on
scan disagreement.
Three things remain unresolved, and the reasons differ. A commissioning map meeting all
four acceptance criteria and localisation against a saved map are blocked by the size of the
available test area, not by the platform. The effect of the asymmetric geometry itself is
unquantified, because no matched symmetric baseline has been built. And several degrees of
heading error survive every instrument currently fitted, narrowed to an encoder or wheel-
radius scale error or a rigid all-wheel slip mode, which cannot be separated without an
independent angular-rate measurement.
The question Year 2 tests follows directly from the last of those. Adding inertial
measurement to a platform whose unfused behaviour is now characterised gives a specific
quantity to test the improvement against, rather than a general expectation that fusion helps.
